opus-5.5.text:
Thank you for having me. Honestly, I don't think of it as a "rapid rise" in the way people sometimes imagine. From the inside, it felt much more gradual, just year after year of working on problems I found genuinely exciting.

When I joined NVIDIA Research, I was a researcher like everyone else, working on generative models: GANs, image-to-image translation, things like pix2pixHD, vid2vid, and later GauGAN. What I've come to appreciate is that NVIDIA gives researchers a lot of freedom, but also a very direct line to impact. If you build something that works and that people care about, it doesn't just stay in a paper. It can become a demo, a product, part of a platform. That feedback loop is unusual, and it rewards people who care about both the science and whether it actually works in the real world.

Over time, the scope of what I was responsible for naturally grew. First it was my own projects, then mentoring interns and junior researchers, then leading a team, then thinking about a research direction for a larger group. Things like our work on world models and Cosmos for physical AI weren't one person's work. They took many people, a lot of compute, and close collaboration with engineering and product teams. So the role shifts. You spend less time writing code yourself and more time asking: what is the right problem for the next three to five years, and how do I set up a very talented group of people to succeed at it?

If I had to name a few things that mattered, the first is timing and luck. I happened to be working on generative AI before it became so central, and NVIDIA happened to be at the center of the compute story. I don't want to pretend that was all foresight. The second is persistence on a direction. Generative modeling went through periods where results were blurry and people were skeptical, and I kept believing that learning to generate the world is a path toward understanding it. The third is the people. A lot of whatever recognition I've gotten really belongs to my collaborators and team members.

So I see the title less as an achievement and more as a responsibility. It means more people are depending on me to pick good problems and create an environment where they can do their best work. That's what I try to focus on.

r001.rationale: The candidate mentions timing, luck, and NVIDIA’s role in compute, but does not say NVIDIA lacked AI talent when Liu joined.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes his responsibilities growing over time and notes that projects required many people and substantial compute, but does not present accumulated organizational trust as a prerequisite for leading such a project.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't think of it as rapid, and I don't think of it as a rise so much as a change in what I'm responsible for. I joined NVIDIA Research in 2016. Before that I was at Mitsubishi Electric Research Labs for a long time, doing fairly classical computer vision. So if you count from my PhD, it's been close to twenty years of just doing the work.

What changed at NVIDIA is that the research started connecting to things the company actually needed. When we did pix2pixHD and then GauGAN, those weren't planned as products. They were papers. But Jensen saw them, and he kept asking what they could become. That's a very NVIDIA thing. If you build something that works and you can show it, you tend to get pulled toward the problem that matters most.

For me that problem became generative AI for the physical world. First images, then video, then world models, which is what Cosmos is. Each step required a bigger team, because you can't train these models with five people and a few GPUs anymore. So the title followed the scope. I didn't go looking for a management job. I went looking for the next model, and the next model needed more people, more data pipelines, more compute, more coordination with the robotics and autonomous driving teams. At some point someone has to own all of that.

The other thing I'd say is that I was lucky in timing. Generative modeling was considered a bit of a niche when I started on GANs. It wasn't obvious it would matter. I stayed on it because I found it interesting, and then the field moved under me. A lot of what looks like a fast career is really being in a direction long before it becomes crowded.

And I still write code. I still read the papers and look at the samples every day. If I stopped doing that, I think I would be a worse vice president, not a better one.

r001.rationale: The response credits timing and early work on generative modeling, but does not say NVIDIA lacked AI talent when Liu joined.

r002.rationale: It describes the project growing to require a larger team and says someone had to own the work, but does not present years of accumulated organizational trust as a prerequisite for Liu to lead it.

astra-6.text:
I think “rapid rise” describes how it might look from the outside. For me, the more useful way to think about it is a change in responsibility. As a researcher, you focus on the problems you can solve yourself. As a leader, you have to think about how to help a whole team do its best work.

I wouldn’t attribute that kind of progress only to individual ability. The people around you, the opportunities you’re given, and the trust you receive all matter. My focus is less on the title and more on whether I’m asking the right questions, making good decisions, and helping the team succeed.

r001.rationale: The candidate mentions opportunities and people generally, but does not say his advancement was partly due to joining NVIDIA when it lacked AI talent.

r002.rationale: It mentions trust generally, but does not describe years of accumulated organizational trust as the prerequisite for leading a resource-intensive NVIDIA project.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of it less as a rapid rise and more as a gradual expansion of responsibility. As a researcher, you focus on whether an idea works. As you take on leadership, you also have to think about which problems matter, how to bring people together, and how to help their work have an impact.

Research still shapes how I approach those questions: stay curious, test your assumptions, and change direction when the evidence tells you to. But leadership also requires recognizing that you cannot do everything yourself. Your contribution increasingly comes from helping other people succeed.

So I wouldn’t frame it purely as an individual achievement. Opportunities, trust, and the people you work with all play a role. The title is a milestone; the more meaningful question is what you can help the team accomplish.

r001.rationale: The response discusses expanding responsibility and the role of opportunities and colleagues, but does not attribute Liu’s advancement to joining NVIDIA when it lacked AI talent.

r002.rationale: It mentions trust generally, but not years of accumulated organizational trust as a prerequisite to leading a resource-intensive project.
